items.title: The way trees sway may communicate water stress
items.desc: The Western U.S. is experiencing periods of increasingly intense drought, and higher temperatures are exacerbating the issue by drawing even more moisture from plants and soils into the atmosphere. The results can be seen in the ever-expanding wildfire footprint, with many of the region's largest recorded wildfires occurring over the past decade. One DRI scientist is innovating a new way to monitor water stress in trees—one that may help monitor wildfire risk across the region.

items.title: Long-sought Zhang-Rice singlet visualized directly in cuprate superconductor
items.desc: Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with zero electrical resistance below specific temperatures. Most of these materials become superconducting at very low temperatures, but some also exhibit superconductivity at higher temperatures.

items.title: New wildfire research system follows ecosystems from controlled burns through long-term recovery
items.desc: On a perfect, crisp fall day with blue skies, scientists in yellow safety coats gather in the sprawling desert north of Reno. They watch as flames consume a burning bush and quickly spread through the surrounding grass. The fire is completely controlled and monitored by dozens of sensors as three enormous drones buzz directly overhead, following the curl of smoke as it dances in the light breeze.

items.title: A transferable framework for evaluating the potential for forecast-informed reservoir operations in watersheds
items.desc: With extreme weather increasing around the world, scientists are working to help critical infrastructure, such as water management systems, adapt. On the U.S. West Coast, where both periods of prolonged drought and intense atmospheric river storms are common, effective water management can be particularly tricky.

items.title: The perfect storm that turbocharged Venezuela's twin quakes
items.desc: A dangerous cocktail of tectonic positioning, loose earth and shoddy construction contributed to the unprecedented damage caused by Venezuela's twin earthquakes, experts say.

items.title: How to design a space habitat that supports its residents' mental health
items.desc: In extreme environments, habitats are built for survival. Submarines, Antarctic bases and post-disaster dwellings are designed to prioritize health and safety. This is especially the case for habitats in space, where room is limited, contact with Earth is remote and hazards are numerous.

items.title: Total solar eclipse to spellbind Europe
items.desc: Millions of Europeans will contemplate the sky in awe on Wednesday as a rare total solar eclipse crosses part of the continent and plunges a swath of Spain into eerie daytime darkness.

items.title: UK 'on course' to record warmest summer for second year in a row
items.desc: Britain is "on course" to chalk up its warmest summer on record for the second year running, the UK's Met Office weather agency said Tuesday as the country braced for its fifth heat wave of the season.

items.title: How Britain's mapmakers track climate change
items.desc: Once used to defend Britain's shores against Napoleonic France, the Ordnance Survey's detailed maps are now essential for tracking and adapting to climate change.

items.title: Elvish, Klingon and Pig Latin: What can invented languages teach us about the human brain?
items.desc: Invented languages tend to be the stuff of fantasy or science fiction worlds. But as a child, you may have made one up yourself.

items.title: Looking to see the solar eclipse from North America? Here's where and when to catch a sliver
items.desc: Sorry, North America. After winning the cosmic lottery with a pair of coast-to-coast total solar eclipses, now it's Europe's turn.

items.title: Today's Mediterranean diet leans on olive oil, veggies and fish—But the ancients mainly ate bread
items.desc: The Roman emperor Julian (332–363 CE) called bread the food that "among us is thought to be the most nourishing."

items.title: Japan's earthquake shows extreme heat can turn one disaster into two
items.desc: Emergency workers attempting to rescue survivors after a recent earthquake in Kyushu, Japan, also had to cope with extreme summer heat.

items.title: The ESCAPE mission will study the evolution of exoplanet atmospheres
items.desc: The habitable zone concept is useful for understanding which worlds might, possibly, maybe, be habitable. It highlights exoplanets at the right distances from their stars for liquid water to potentially exist on their surfaces. But that alone can't determine habitability.

items.title: Archaeology has evolved: Four eras of understanding Africa's past
items.desc: What is the past? It may seem a simple question to answer, but it is more complex than we might think at first. As science, politics, technologies and ways of thinking change, so does our understanding of what went before.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch inside silver nanocatalysts
items.desc: Silver nanocatalysts have been found to switch where they perform their most important reactions depending on whether a solid oxide cell is making electricity or hydrogen. The discovery could enable smarter catalyst designs that boost clean power generation while making green hydrogen more energy-efficient.

items.title: The sun will vanish over Europe in a rare total solar eclipse: Watch live
items.desc: A total solar eclipse will plunge parts of Europe into darkness on August 12, 2026, with Spain offering some of the best views. ESA will livestream the spectacle from the Javalambre Observatory, combining telescope feeds, drone footage, and expert commentary. At 20:31 CEST, the observatory will experience 1 minute and 21 seconds of totality, revealing the Sun’s normally hidden outer atmosphere.

items.title: For 15,000 years, humans and dogs have been changing each other
items.desc: Dogs have been shaping—and being shaped by—humans for about 15,000 years, evolving from early partners of hunter-gatherers into an astonishing range of specialized companions. Across the globe, they adapted alongside people to wildly different environments and needs, from powerful Arctic sled dogs and agile rainforest hunters to high-altitude dogs with genetic traits for surviving thin air. Some were even bred for wool, while others played important spiritual or ceremonial roles.

items.title: 60,000-year-old ostrich eggshell engravings reveal a surprisingly sophisticated human mind
items.desc: More than 60,000 years ago, humans in southern Africa were engraving ostrich eggshells with intricate geometric patterns that appear far more organized than previously realized. Researchers found recurring grids, parallel lines, right angles, and repeated shapes, suggesting the designs followed deliberate rules rather than being improvised. The engravers may even have planned entire patterns in their minds before carving them.

items.title: Potatoes may have given Indigenous Andeans a digestive superpower
items.desc: The rise of the potato in the Andes appears to have left a lasting mark on human DNA. Indigenous Peruvians carry exceptionally high numbers of a starch-digestion gene, likely because people with more copies gained an evolutionary advantage once potatoes became a staple food. The change began thousands of years before European contact, providing unusually strong evidence that diet can shape human evolution.

items.title: 240-million-year-old reptile fossil reveals a lost chapter before dinosaurs and crocodiles
items.desc: A 240-million-year-old reptile discovered in Brazil is revealing what evolution looked like just before the rise of dinosaurs and crocodiles. The small predator had unusually positioned legs that may have allowed it to move more efficiently than many earlier reptiles. Its close relatives were previously known mostly from other continents, suggesting these ancient animals spread much farther across the Triassic world than scientists realized.

items.title: Cassini reveals a surprising twist in Saturn’s magnetic shield
items.desc: Cassini data has revealed a surprising twist in Saturn’s magnetic shield: the planet’s rapid rotation appears to drag a key opening in its magnetosphere far toward the afternoon side instead of keeping it near noon, as happens on Earth. The finding confirms that giant planets like Saturn operate under a fundamentally different magnetic regime, where fast spin and charged material from moons such as Enceladus can overpower the Sun’s influence.

items.title: Stress can scramble your brain’s internal GPS, MRI study finds
items.desc: Stress may literally scramble the brain’s internal GPS. Researchers found that cortisol, a hormone released during stress, made people significantly worse at navigating a virtual environment and disrupted the precise activity of grid cells, specialized brain cells that help us understand where we are in space. When landmarks were missing, this navigation system nearly stopped functioning, while another brain region appeared to step in and compensate.

items.title: Scientists discover bacteria that lock toxic uranium into a stable form
items.desc: Deep underground, bacteria may be capable of doing something remarkable: trapping toxic uranium before it spreads. When researchers fed microbes in uranium-contaminated mine water with glycerol, about 95% of the dissolved uranium disappeared within 130 days. The bacteria helped convert it into an unusually stable uranium compound that had rarely been observed before.

items.title: Chemists set electrons free and break a decades-old chemistry barrier
items.desc: Chemists have developed a catalyst that breaks a long-standing rule governing which molecules receive electrons during chemical reactions. By releasing electrons directly into solution, the technique could unlock reactions—and potentially useful new molecules—that were previously out of reach.

items.title: Meteorite that smashed through a New Jersey roof reveals clues to life’s origins
items.desc: A rare meteorite that crashed through a New Jersey roof contains evidence of ancient salty fluids, organic compounds, and amino acids from a primitive asteroid. Its pristine chemistry could offer new clues about how space rocks helped supply early Earth with some of the ingredients needed for life.

items.title: The dodo bird had a secret sensory world scientists are only now discovering
items.desc: CT scans of the world’s rarest dodo skulls suggest the extinct bird may have had a stronger sense of smell, a highly sensitive beak, and a lifestyle that extended into dawn and dusk. The discoveries are helping overturn centuries-old myths and reveal a far more complex animal than the famously “dumb” dodo of popular imagination.

items.title: The sun is covered in tiny whirlpools we’ve never seen before
items.desc: Scientists have discovered incredibly tiny plasma whirlpools swirling across the Sun’s surface, some just 20 kilometers wide. These previously invisible vortices may twist magnetic fields and help build up the energy released in small solar eruptions called nanoflares. They may also help magnetic fields spread through the Sun’s atmosphere far faster than current models can explain.

items.title: Dinosaurs became giants — so why did they never become tiny?
items.desc: Dinosaurs conquered the land at enormous sizes, but strangely, they almost never evolved into truly tiny animals. New research suggests that physiology alone can’t explain this missing miniature end of the dinosaur spectrum—and that early mammals may have been partly responsible. While dinosaurs kept mammals from becoming large, small mammals may have returned the favor by occupying ecological niches that could otherwise have supported mouse-sized dinosaurs.

items.title: Sunlight creates quantum entanglement once thought to require lasers
items.desc: Scientists have generated quantum entanglement directly from sunlight, potentially offering a lower-energy alternative to the lasers normally used in quantum technology. Their outdoor experiment produced entangled photons with about 94% similarity to an ideal state. The result could pave the way for simpler quantum satellites, secure communications, and more energy-efficient quantum computing.

items.title: The Monetary Roots of Political Extremism
items.desc: While the global economy generates unprecedented wealth for plutocrats like Elon Musk, it is, by design, highly unequal, dangerously over-indebted, prone to recurring financial crises, and ecologically disastrous. In such a context, radical reforms will be needed, beginning with the rejection of money as a commodity.

items.title: The Return of the Power Trust
items.desc: A century ago, the US power industry was dominated by sprawling, heavily indebted holding companies until their collapse forced the federal government to break them up. Now, the pattern is repeating, with mega-mergers and buyouts advancing a debt-heavy business model at the expense of households and communities.

items.title: Morocco’s Bet on Targeted AI
items.desc: Rather than join the global race for computing power, Morocco has focused on building sovereignty over its data, talent, and uses of AI, because technological power will be measured by usefulness, not by domination. This strategy calls for the country to embrace innovation without ceding its identity to foreign models.

items.title: Dude, Where’s My Recession?
items.desc: Despite a series of major negative shocks, some of them unprecedented, the US economy continues to grow in line with its estimated long-run potential. Yet given obvious and mounting risks, from debt-financed speculation to geopolitical tensions, the appearance of resilience should not be confused with the real thing.

items.title: The Rise of the Token Economy
items.desc: Millions of people continuously generate the raw material on which AI is trained, yet almost none shares in the wealth it creates. This underscores the need for data cooperatives representing internet users, creators, and other rights holders to negotiate access to the content being fed to large language models.

items.title: Excess Savings Are Driving the New China Shock
items.desc: The current China shock combines continued supply upgrading with an absorption problem: the decline in property and related investment has reduced domestic demand, but national saving remains very high. The result is a larger savings-investment surplus that spills into net exports.

items.title: The World Economy Is Swerving, and the Destination Is Unknown
items.desc: The days of unfettered globalization, multilateral rule of law, commonly accepted limits on economic statecraft, and widely shared macroeconomic objectives are now long gone. A perpetual, directionless transition is our new reality, and corporate executives, investors, and policymakers must adapt accordingly.

items.title: Is China Really a Beggar-thy-Neighbor Power?
items.desc: When major economies are running at near full capacity, it is not clear that trade deficits should be a cause for concern, since they represent a transfer of purchasing power from surplus countries. Under the current circumstances, then, China’s widely criticized surpluses might as well be called enrich-thy-neighbor.

items.title: No Escape from the Russian Terror Playbook
items.desc: When Vladimir Putin revives Stalin-era repression tactics, he does not do so in service of some lofty ideology or grand project. Rather, he and his security apparatus are seeking to safeguard their own power indefinitely—and, as Russians well know, they will stop at nothing to succeed.

items.title: The Extractive Trap Has a Green Exit
items.desc: For resource-rich developing countries, decades of resource extraction have produced income concentration, economic dependency, external vulnerabilities, and the weakening of other productive sectors. Achieving broad-based prosperity requires a new approach, one which leverages South-South cooperation to build green industries.

items.title: The Last Trump Election
items.desc: No matter what US President Donald Trump says or does in response to the results of this November’s midterms, he will have faced his final popular vote. There will be further damage done to public confidence in American democratic institutions, but the institutions themselves will hold.

items.title: The Ceuta Crisis Is About More Than Migration
items.desc: When tens of thousands of people recently entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from neighboring Morocco, European leaders lapsed into recriminations, reigniting the debate on migration. But the bigger challenge is to address a long-simmering territorial dispute between Spain and Morocco.

items.title: The Rising Price of a Cheap Renminbi
items.desc: Renminbi appreciation would not, on its own, rebalance China’s economy and eliminate its massive surpluses. But by increasing households’ purchasing power over imports and compressing tradable-sector margins, it would raise the cost of avoiding reform.

items.title: Who Should Build the Low-Carbon Economy?
items.desc: Since the first Industrial Revolution, goods and technologies have reached the farthest corners of the world, but the ability to design, build, market, and extract value from them has remained highly concentrated. Unless humanity can break this pattern, a sufficient response to climate change will remain out of reach.

items.title: Will Iceland Rejoin the EU Path?
items.desc: US President Donald Trump’s volatile and unpredictable security policies, particularly his desire to control Greenland, have put Iceland in a vulnerable position. This uncomfortable reality will likely be front of mind as voters decide whether to reopen membership negotiations with the European Union.

items.title: The community healthcare model transforming lives across West Africa
items.desc: In parts of West Africa, getting sick used to mean navigating a maze of barriers — distance, cost, time spent away from work — before ever seeing a health worker. If one AI agent can eventually supervise 100 other agents, “AI as a coworker” is probably a temporary phase. The end state looks more like an organization.
The most dangerous assumption in the AI debate is that productivity gains automatically make everyone richer. History gives us absolutely no reason to assume that.

We’re at the point where someone can use ChatGPT + Codex + genomics tools to help design a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine for their dog. That sentence would’ve sounded like sci-fi a year ago. The tools ordinary people suddenly have access to are absolutely insane.
If AI makes software, design, law, accounting and analysis radically cheaper, a lot of “prestigious” careers are about to find out how much of their value came from scarcity.
I think the first major AI labor crisis will hit young people, not older workers. Why hire ten juniors to learn the job when one senior with AI can do the output of the whole team?
The most important number in robotics will not be IQ, benchmark scores or walking speed. It will be cost per productive hour. Once that number beats humans, everything changes.
The scary part about superhuman AI is not that it might hate us. It is that it could completely transform the economy while feeling absolutely nothing about who wins and who loses.
We may discover that the hardest part of building a post-work society was never the technology. It was convincing people that a human life does not need to be economically productive to be valuable.
